title: Ethics and data journalism: adding a new dimension to the data journalism pyramid
content:
Here’s a version of the inverted pyramid of data journalism that shows ethical considerations at each stage, thanks to the research of Laurence Dierickx, Marilia Gehrke and Carl-Gustav Linden which I blogged about yesterday.

The research maps the stages of the pyramid of data journalism to different categories and ethical justifications.

I’ve also added some others.

Privacy, for example, is listed in the research in relation to compiling data, but it is also a (potentially bigger) concern in communication: for example you might choose to use a heatmap instead of a points map to avoid identifying individuals, so in my diagram I’ve included privacy in both.

I’ve also included mentioned uncertainty in communication, as this is a major issue in data visualisation and journalism more generally.

Verification is listed in the research in relation to the compile stage, but it might also be one of the reasons for combining data or putting it into context: both stages might involve checking data against a second source.

Cleaning also often involves checking for outliers that may have been misentered, and duplication

title: Are newsroom guidelines fit for purpose when it comes to data journalism?
content:
News organisations’ guidelines haven’t kept up with developments in data-driven journalism, they need to learn from practices in other fields — and principles need to be embedded in practice, according to new research on data journalism ethics.

Researchers Laurence Dierickx, Marilia Gehrke and Carl-Gustav Linden looked at dozens of European news organisations’ ethical codes to see how they relate to each stage of the Data Journalism Pyramid. They conclude that while ethical codes might talk in general about ethical principles, they rarely provide any guidance on how to apply those in practice when it comes to data-driven reporting.

Underpinning the research is the concept of ‘epistemic governance‘: the idea that an individual journalist is not solely responsible for the ethics of newsroom output.

This “governance perspective”, they write, “asks how ethical obligations become embedded in the procedural architecture of journalistic workflows, shifting ethics from values to be held to conditions to be built into practice”.

title: I built a game to help learn how to choose good interviewees
content:
Earlier this year I published the PEER technique for brainstorming interviewees: “four categories to help journalists generate more names on any given story — and think more creatively about whose voices might add something to that story.”

Now I’ve built a game to put that technique into practice — and improve your sourcing.

It’s much more fun.

Who should you call? has seven levels that move from identifying the type of source, to identifying who is missing from a story, to finding under-represented voices and picking a full interview list.

I included a ‘Blue vs Red’ teams mode for using the game in a class or training session. This allows you to introduce a competitive element by splitting a class into two teams. The lecturer can host a whole-class game on a big screen or let students play it themselves in smaller teams.

Play switches from one team to another when a team gets a question wrong. But play also switches if a team gets three answers correct in a row, to avoid the other team getting bored.

The game keeps track of each team’s scores and gives a running total at the end of each round.

title: Using personalisation makes every AI chat less risky and more effective — here are five essential custom instructions to add
content:
One of best things you can do to lower the risks of using AI and improve the quality of outputs is to spend five minutes with one of AI tools’ least-used features: their personalisation settings.

ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Claude all have personalisation features: a section of the tool where you can give it permanent extra information that informs every conversation. You can find it in your general settings under names like ‘instructions’, ‘personal context’ or ‘personalization’, or using the links above.

Here are five instructions you can include in that section:

Your professional role, ethics, location, language, skill level and other details all provide vital context that will help reduce assumptions and misunderstandings and improve the ‘predictions’ that AI tools make when responding.

title: How to judge (and minimise) the risk of using sensitive information with an AI chatbot
content:
One of the most common misunderstandings about large language models (LLMs) is the idea that if you upload a document such as an interview transcript, confidential leak or sensitive dataset to an AI tool like ChatGPT, it might reveal that document to another user.

There are no publicly documented cases of this happening.

The reason for this is the same reason why AI shouldn’t be treated as a search engine: large language models like GPT-5 don’t work by retrieving documents for users — they work by separating documents into parts of language (‘tokens’ in the jargon), adding those to a vast ocean of other tokens, and training on a database of relationships between those.

When you ask a question like “Who is the CEO of Apple?” a genAI tool doesn’t retrieve information from a document. Instead it breaks down your question into tokens like “CEO” and “Apple” and “Who”, calculates the most statistically likely meaning of those things (e.g. is that apple probably a fruit or a company), and then the most statistically likely sequence of words which might form a meaningful answer to that question.

title: How data journalism is done on TikTok: six key takeaways from watching 50 videos
content:
Short-form vertical video is quickly becoming a key format for telling all types of news stories — and data journalism is no exception.

As a data journalist, I wanted to know how these outlets use this new and evolving digital video format to create “data shorts”: short-form social media videos in a vertical, reel-style format, that analyses or reports on specific datasets or newly released data.

I analysed 50 data shorts from the TikTok accounts of five major UK news publications — the BBC, ITV News, Guardian, Times and Financial Times — to examine how these digital news outlets approach the format. I looked at the genre of story they covered, the angles they focused on, their length, and their use of animation, to help inform my guidelines.

My analysed data shorts averaged a runtime of just under 84 seconds.

The BBC ranked lowest for average video length, at just under a minute, while the Financial Times had the highest at 105 seconds.

Notably, none of the publications had an average video length over two minutes, despite TikTok allowing longer uploads up to 60 minutes.

title: This one story can be used to discuss seven different types of bias
content:
The latest “wife of” headline — ITV News’s report on the actor Lisa Faulkner revealing that she has undergone surgery after a cancer diagnosis — is an opportunity to get journalism students exploring how different forms of bias might shape news reporting — and not just the obvious ones.

An opening question might be why a reporter or editor would put another person’s name at the front of the headline “John Torode’s wife Lisa Faulkner reveals breast cancer diagnosis”.

A male-dominated newsroom might be one answer. Another might be a newsroom that is more likely to watch a middle-class cooking programme (Masterchef) than a working-class soap opera (Eastenders). It might also be driven by search analytics: four times as many searches were made for Torode in the last 12 months than Faulkner.

Search analytics are closely related to bias around news values: why, for example, might reporting lead on “Taylor Swift’s boyfriend” or “Nicole Kidman’s husband” instead? How do news values come into play with Amal Clooney or Meghan Markle or The Chicago Tribune leading on the bronze medal-winning “Wife of a Bears’ lineman“? And how do they intersect with other forces?

title: Managing a mass FOI project? Here’s an AI-assisted methodology for that
content:
Sending FOIs to multiple bodies across the country to get the big picture on an issue sounds like a great idea — until the responses start to trickle in. Differences between responses often make mass FOI projects extremely time-consuming as you try to get everything into a format that allows you to ask journalistic questions and compare different authorities. Can AI help?

On one recent project I decided to put together a methodology that made the process less stressful, faster and more accurate. Here’s how it works.

The main problem journalists face with responses to a bulk FOI request is their inconsistency. This can be reduced by specifying the year used (financial or calendar), the format of the response (spreadsheet) and even providing a template, but inevitably some authorities will ignore either or both.

title: Showing charts on video? Here are two essential techniques to make them effective
content:
Using visualisation on TV and video is very different to using charts and maps online. In video, the audience has very little time to absorb the information contained in the chart — so you need to get them to that information as quickly as possible.

Every bad example of charts in videos forgets this. And every good example uses two essential techniques: keeping things simple, and adding motion.

Viewers looking at an on-screen chart have to take in at least three types of information in a short space of time: shapes (bars, slices, lines, etc.), colours, and text (titles, subtitles, labels, annotations and legends).

The more you can reduce the time needed to interpret each of those, the quicker the viewer can understand the chart.

The best place to start is reducing the number of data points to those that are absolutely essential. This will reduce the number of shapes the viewer has to absorb.

If your story is about ranking the worst or best areas for a problem, for example, a top ten is too much for video. Cut back to just the top three or five.

title: “Many newsrooms are not optimised for what humans do best” (but we have an opportunity to change that)
content:
Some essential reading by Agnes Stenbom Swedling explores how news organisations integrate AI into their workflows and the idea of the “human in the loop“. Many newsrooms, she points out, “are not optimised for what humans do best”, and so far the introduction of AI hasn’t involved a critical consideration of whether we want to embed those features in new systems, or rethink them:

“What is being built – incrementally, often unintentionally – is a form of machine-centric hybridisation. Workflows are optimised for what machines do well: speed, scale, pattern recognition, cost efficiency. Humans are then positioned around those systems, adapting their tasks, roles, and decision-making to fit the logics of machines. 

“The consequence is a subtle but significant inversion: rather than engaging in uniquely human activities, work is reorganised to fit machine-driven processes. And once that inversion is embedded at the infrastructural level, it becomes increasingly difficult to reverse.”
